title: Macroeconomic objectives
summary: Governments aim for economic growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation and sustainable public debt. Each objective has causes, costs and trade-offs. HL adds price-index and unemployment calculations and the Phillips curve.

keyterms.definition: An increase in real GDP over time, from rising AD (actual growth) or rising productive capacity (potential growth).
People of working age who are able, available and actively looking for work but do not have a job.
Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers’ skills or location and available jobs, e.g. after an industry declines.
Short-term unemployment while people move between jobs.
Unemployment caused by a fall in AD during a downturn.
Unemployment when the economy is at full employment: frictional + structural + seasonal.
A sustained rise in the average price level, usually measured by the consumer price index (CPI).
A sustained fall in the average price level (negative inflation).
A fall in the rate of inflation: prices still rise, but more slowly.
Inflation caused by AD rising faster than the economy’s capacity to produce.
Inflation caused by rising costs of production, e.g. wages or imported energy, shifting SRAS left.
The total amount a government owes, the accumulation of past budget deficits; often shown as a % of GDP.
A price index where each item’s price change is weighted by its share of household spending.
The short-run inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment; in the long run the curve is vertical at the natural rate.

questions.prompt: Which is a cost of economic growth?
questions.explanation: Growth can harm the environment and may increase inequality.

questions.text: A labour force of 25 million with 1.5 million unemployed has an unemployment rate of ___%.

questions.prompt: Match each case to the type of unemployment.

pairs.left: Graduate searching for a first job
Factory workers laid off in a recession

questions.explanation: Identifying the cause tells you which policy fits.

questions.statement: Cyclical unemployment is best reduced by policies that raise aggregate demand.
questions.explanation: It is caused by deficient demand, so demand-side policy is appropriate.

questions.prompt: Which policy best addresses structural unemployment?
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment needs supply-side measures that fix the skills or location mismatch.

questions.text: Unemployment at full employment (frictional + structural + seasonal) is the ___ rate of unemployment.
questions.explanation: Even at full employment some unemployment remains.

questions.statement: The official unemployment rate may understate true unemployment because of hidden unemployment and underemployment.
questions.explanation: Discouraged workers and part-timers wanting full-time work are not fully captured.

questions.prompt: Which is a consequence of high unemployment?
options: Lost output and lower tax revenue
questions.explanation: Unemployment wastes resources, raises welfare costs and harms individuals.

options: A parent choosing to stay at home
A 30-year-old actively searching and available for work
questions.explanation: They must be able, available and actively seeking work.

questions.prompt: Order the chain of a recession raising unemployment.
questions.explanation: Labour is a derived demand: it depends on demand for output.

questions.prompt: Which is the best example of disinflation?
questions.explanation: Disinflation is a slower rate of price increases, not falling prices.

questions.statement: Deflation always benefits an economy because goods become cheaper.
questions.explanation: Consumers may delay purchases, debt burdens rise in real terms and firms cut output and jobs.

questions.prompt: Match each cause to the type of inflation.

pairs.left: Large rise in government spending at full capacity

questions.explanation: Demand-pull comes from AD; cost-push from SRAS shifting left.

questions.text: Inflation caused by rising production costs is ___ inflation.
questions.explanation: Cost-push shifts SRAS left, raising the price level and reducing output.

questions.prompt: Who is most likely to lose from unexpected inflation?
options: Savers whose interest rate is below inflation
questions.explanation: Inflation erodes the real value of savings and fixed incomes.

questions.prompt: Why do many central banks target low, positive inflation (around 2%) rather than zero?
options: It avoids the risks of deflation and gives room for real interest rates to fall
It is required by the IMF
questions.explanation: A small buffer above zero helps avoid deflationary spirals.

questions.statement: Government debt is the accumulation of past budget deficits.
questions.explanation: Each year’s deficit adds to the stock of debt.

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of very high government debt?
options: Lower interest rates for all borrowers
Rising interest payments that crowd out other spending
questions.explanation: Debt servicing has an opportunity cost and may lead to credit downgrades.

questions.text: A sustained fall in the average price level is ___.
questions.explanation: Deflation can be caused by falling AD (bad) or rising AS (benign).

items: Incomes fall and prices fall further
questions.explanation: Expectations of falling prices can feed on themselves.

lessons.title: HL: Price indices and the Phillips curve

questions.prompt: Basket weights: food 40, housing 35, transport 25. Price indices: food 105, housing 110, transport 96. What is the weighted CPI?

questions.text: A CPI that rises from 125 to 130 shows an inflation rate of ___%.

questions.statement: Weights in a CPI reflect the share of household spending on each item.
questions.explanation: Items that take a larger share of the budget have more effect on measured inflation.

options: a positive relationship between inflation and unemployment
that unemployment is always at its natural rate
the link between growth and debt
an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment
questions.explanation: Lower unemployment tends to be accompanied by higher inflation in the short run.

questions.statement: In the long run, the Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
questions.explanation: Once expectations adjust, there is no lasting trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

questions.prompt: According to the expectations-augmented Phillips curve, what happens if government holds unemployment below the natural rate?
options: Unemployment stays low with stable inflation
Inflation keeps accelerating as expectations rise
questions.explanation: Workers expect higher inflation, the SRPC shifts up, and only accelerating inflation keeps unemployment below the natural rate.

questions.text: Labour force 32 million, employed 30.4 million. The unemployment rate is ___%.

questions.prompt: Which problem limits the accuracy of the CPI?
options: It uses no data on prices
Quality improvements and new products are hard to account for
questions.explanation: The basket may not reflect individual spending, and quality changes bias the index.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its description.
questions.explanation: Stagflation in the 1970s challenged the simple Phillips curve.

questions.prompt: Order the shift in a short-run Phillips curve.
items: Unemployment falls below the natural rate and inflation rises
Workers expect higher inflation and demand higher wages
SRPC shifts up and unemployment returns to the natural rate
questions.explanation: This explains why the long-run Phillips curve is vertical.
